stem: Neural networks take numbers, and words are not numbers. What are the two steps that get a sentence into a transformer?
choices: Spell-check it, then translate it into English
Hash each word to an integer, then sort the integers
Split it into tokens, then embed each token as a vector of numbers whose position carries the word's meaning
Count how often each word occurs, then normalise the counts
explanation: Tokenise, then embed. Tokenising chops the text into units the model has a vocabulary for; embedding maps each unit to a vector, so that words with related meanings sit near one another.

stem: What does it mean that word embeddings support 'word algebra', as in king minus male plus female giving queen?
choices: The model stores a dictionary of analogies collected from the training text
Directions in the embedding space correspond to consistent relationships, so the offset that separates male words from female words is roughly the same vector everywhere
Words are assigned numbers in alphabetical order, so arithmetic on them preserves order
Each word is stored as the sum of the letters it contains
explanation: The geometry itself carries meaning. Because gender, tense and plurality each show up as a consistent direction, adding and subtracting vectors moves you along those relationships — which is why nothing about analogies had to be programmed in.

stem: What is the difference between an embedding and attention?
choices: An embedding is computed during training; attention is computed by hand
An embedding applies to words; attention applies to images
An embedding gives a word its global-context meaning as a vector; attention gives it a local-context interpretation relative to the other words in this particular sentence
An embedding is a layer; attention is a loss function
explanation: The embedding of 'bank' is the same wherever it appears — it carries what the word means in general. Attention is what decides that in 'the bank of the river' the neighbouring words should pull that meaning towards the shore rather than the vault.

stem: What does the T in ChatGPT stand for?
explanation: Transformer — the architecture underneath. GPT is Generative Pre-trained Transformer: generative because it produces new text, pre-trained because it learns from a corpus before any task, transformer because attention lets it weigh every other token when choosing the next one.

stem: GPT stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformer. What does the 'pre-trained' part mean?
choices: The model was trained on internet-scale text before being put to any particular task, so it arrives already knowing the language
The model was trained by a previous generation of researchers and inherited unchanged
The weights were initialised to sensible values before training rather than at random
The model is trained again from scratch before each conversation
explanation: Pre-training is the expensive general phase: predict the next token over a huge corpus, and language competence falls out. Everything after that — instruction tuning, a specific task — adapts a model that already exists.

stem: How does a transformer decide which word it generates next?
choices: It looks up the most common word that follows the previous one in its training corpus
It searches its training data for the closest matching sentence and copies the next word from it
It generates several complete sentences and picks the shortest

It embeds and positionally encodes the tokens, uses attention to weigh how much every other token should inform each one, and outputs a probability distribution over the whole vocabulary from which the next token is sampled
explanation: Embed, position, attend, then a distribution over the vocabulary. The model never chooses a word outright: it produces probabilities for all of them and one is sampled, which is why the same prompt can give different answers.

stem: Select the components that are genuinely main parts of a transformer as this course describes it.
choices: Token embedding
Positional encoding
Convolutional filters slid across the token sequence
Self-attention layers
A recurrent loop that feeds each hidden state into the next step
explanation: Embedding, positional encoding and attention are the transformer's parts, with a feedforward block and an output softmax alongside them. Convolution belongs to the CNN, and the absence of recurrence is precisely what the transformer replaced.

stem: Attention looks at every token at once, in no particular order. What problem does positional encoding solve?
choices: It records where the model is in the conversation so it can remember earlier turns
It stores the position of each word in the vocabulary list
It marks which tokens the model is allowed to attend to and which are masked
It tells the model where each token sits in the sequence, since without it 'the dog bit the man' and 'the man bit the dog' would be the same bag of tokens
explanation: Attention is order-blind by construction: it weighs relationships, not sequence. Positional encoding adds the missing information to each token's vector, so word order survives into the representation.

stem: Attention is built from three roles, usually written Q, K and V. What are they, in plain terms?
choices: Question, knowledge and verification — the three stages of answering a prompt
Quantity, keyword and vocabulary — the three statistics kept per token
The query is what a token is looking for, the key is what each other token offers, and the value is the content passed along when a query and a key match well
Quick, keep and verbose — three decoding speeds the model can run at
explanation: Query, key, value. Matching queries against keys produces the weights, and the weighted mixture of values is what each token takes away — so attention is a learned, content-based lookup rather than a fixed wiring.

stem: One word: name the mechanism that lets each token in a sentence weigh how much every other token should inform its interpretation.
explanation: Attention. It is what the 2017 paper title claims is all you need, and it supplies local context: the same embedded word is read differently depending on which other words are present and how strongly they weigh on it.

stem: Why did the transformer displace the recurrent network for language?
choices: A recurrent network cannot be trained by backpropagation, but a transformer can

A recurrent network passes information along one step at a time, so distant words are hard to relate and the computation cannot be parallelised; attention connects every token to every other in one step
Recurrent networks cannot handle vocabularies larger than a few thousand words
The transformer needs no training data, so it scaled faster
explanation: Two wins at once: long-range dependencies become direct rather than relayed, and the sequence can be processed in parallel instead of in order. That parallelism is what made internet-scale pre-training affordable.

stem: Which paper introduced the transformer, and in which year?
choices: Mikolov and colleagues, 2013, 'Efficient Estimation of Word Representations'
Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton, 2012, on ImageNet classification
Vaswani and colleagues, 2017, 'Attention Is All You Need'
Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams, 1986, on learning representations by back-propagating errors
explanation: Vaswani et al., 2017. It is the T in GPT, and it sits on the language timeline directly after word2vec in 2013 and directly before GPT in 2018.

stem: What is the embedding dimension of a large GPT model, as quoted in this course, and what does that number count?
choices: 12,288 — the number of numbers used to represent a single token
12,288 — the number of tokens the model can hold in its context
512 — the number of attention layers stacked in the model
175 billion — the number of words in the vocabulary
explanation: About 12,288 (written 12288) numbers per token. That is the width of the vector a single word occupies, which is what gives an embedding room to encode many independent aspects of meaning at once, and it is why cat sits nearer dog than dinosaur.

stem: What is a large language model, in one sentence?
choices: Any AI system that can hold a conversation, whatever is inside it
A database of language rules assembled by linguists and queried at run time
A model that translates between a large number of languages
A transformer with very many parameters, pre-trained on internet-scale text to predict the next token, which is then used to generate language
explanation: Architecture plus scale plus objective: a transformer, very large, trained to predict the next token on a very large corpus. Everything it appears to know is a by-product of getting good at that one prediction task.

stem: A translation transformer has both an encoder and a decoder, but GPT is described as decoder-only. What does that difference reflect?
choices: GPT is smaller, so one of the two halves was removed to save memory
GPT generates images rather than text, so it needs no encoder

Translation reads a complete source sentence and writes a different one, so it encodes then decodes. GPT continues the text it is given, so a single stack that attends to what came before and predicts what comes next is enough
The encoder is only needed when the model is trained with labels
explanation: The shape of the task sets the shape of the model. Two sequences in two languages call for encoder and decoder; one continuing sequence calls for a single stack predicting the next token.

stem: A word-level translation model reserves a special unknown token. What problem is it there to solve?
choices: It marks the end of a sentence so the decoder knows when to stop
It hides words the model is not allowed to attend to during training
It stores words the model has not yet finished learning
It gives the model a symbol for any word outside its fixed vocabulary, so an unseen word degrades one position rather than breaking the input
explanation: A vocabulary is finite and language is not. Mapping everything unseen to one catch-all token keeps the input well-formed, at the cost of losing whatever that word meant — which is why modern models use sub-word tokens instead.

stem: Why is the language timeline treated as central in this course, even for people who care about images?
choices: Because text files are smaller than images, so more training data is available
Because language is how we communicate, and anything else — including a picture — can be described in words, so a model of language becomes a general interface
Because images cannot be tokenised
Because attention was invented for text and has never been applied to vision
explanation: Language turned out to be the general medium. Once text could be embedded and attended over, the same machinery could be pointed at images, audio and code — which is how the transformer became the backbone of multimodal models.

stem: A transformer chooses the single most probable next word every time, which is why its answers are consistent.
choices: True
False
explanation: False. The output is a probability distribution over the vocabulary and the next token is sampled from it, so the same prompt can produce different continuations. Always taking the most probable token is one option, and it makes output repetitive rather than better.

stem: One word: what are the units a sentence is chopped into before a transformer embeds it?
explanation: Tokens. A token is usually a word or a fragment of one, drawn from a fixed vocabulary, and everything the model does — embedding, attention, prediction — happens over tokens rather than over letters or whole sentences.

stem: In what sense is a generative language model still doing prediction?
choices: It predicts which of its training documents the user is thinking of
It is not predicting at all; generation and prediction are unrelated operations

It predicts the probability of the next token given everything before it, and generates by sampling that prediction and repeating — which is why the course says generative AI is built on predictive AI
It predicts the user's next question so it can prepare the answer in advance
explanation: Generation here is repeated prediction plus sampling. That is the loop the course points at when it says predictive and generative AI are not opposites: the generative model is a next-token predictor run forward.

stem: Which sequence places the language-AI milestones in the right order?
choices: Turing's imitation game, symbolic AI and expert systems, word2vec, the transformer, GPT
Symbolic AI, Turing's imitation game, the transformer, word2vec, GPT
Word2vec, Turing's imitation game, symbolic AI, GPT, the transformer
Turing's imitation game, word2vec, symbolic AI, GPT, the transformer
explanation: Turing 1950, then decades of rule-based expert systems later retronymed GOFAI, then word2vec in 2013 turning words into vectors, then the transformer in 2017, then GPT from 2018. Vectorising the words had to come before attention could weigh them.

stem: 'Attention is all you need' is a strong claim. What was it claiming you no longer need?
choices: Training data, because attention lets a model generalise from a handful of examples
Recurrence and convolution — the sequential and local mechanisms previous sequence models were built on
Embeddings, because attention operates directly on raw characters
A loss function, because attention weights are computed rather than learned
explanation: The title is about what was thrown away. Stripping out recurrence and convolution and keeping only attention plus feedforward layers was the move, and it is what made models trainable at scale.

stem: One word: what is the vector that carries a word's general meaning, and in which similar words sit close together, called?
explanation: An embedding. It gives a word its global-context meaning as a position in a high-dimensional space; attention is the separate mechanism that then adjusts that meaning for the particular sentence the word is in.

stem: Beside attention, each Transformer block contains a feed-forward sub-block. What is it made of?
choices: A second attention layer with its own queries and keys
A recurrent layer that carries state between tokens
A convolution over neighbouring tokens
An up-projection into a much wider dimension, a ReLU nonlinearity, and a down-projection back to the embedding dimension
explanation: Widen, threshold, narrow again. It is an ordinary multilayer perceptron applied to each token separately — which is why the MLP is called the backbone of the Transformer rather than a relic of an older architecture.

stem: Attention and the feed-forward block inside a Transformer do different jobs. What is the division of labour?
choices: Attention moves information between tokens; the feed-forward block acts as a key-value memory that retrieves stored facts and adds them to the token's representation
Attention stores the facts; the feed-forward block routes them between tokens
Attention handles the first half of the sentence and the feed-forward block the second
Attention trains the network while the feed-forward block runs at inference only
explanation: Attention is communication, the feed-forward block is recall. That is why work on where a language model's world knowledge lives points at the feed-forward layers rather than at attention.

stem: In a large language model, the lower and upper layers turn out to store different things. Which way round?
choices: Lower layers store facts and upper layers store grammar
Lower layers store syntactic and shallow patterns; upper layers store deeper semantic world knowledge and facts
Both store the same information, duplicated for robustness
Lower layers store the prompt and upper layers store the answer
explanation: Shallow patterns first, world knowledge later — the same layer-by-layer abstraction the digit network shows with pixels, edges and shapes. It is one more instance of depth buying hierarchy.

stem: What is superposition, in the context of a language model's internal representations?
choices: Two models trained on the same data and averaged
The same token appearing twice in one sentence
Far more concepts than there are dimensions, packed as overlapping nearly-orthogonal directions in one vector space — which is why a single neuron does not correspond to a single concept
Stacking several attention heads on top of each other
explanation: A hundred-dimensional space can carry far more than a hundred distinguishable directions if you accept that they are only nearly perpendicular. The consequence for interpretability is that concepts are smeared across neurons rather than housed in them.

stem: What kind of model is used to pull apart the superposed concepts inside a language model's activations?
choices: A sparse autoencoder, which re-encodes the activations into a much wider but mostly inactive representation so individual concepts separate out
A second Transformer trained on the first one's weights
A convolutional network applied to the attention matrix
A generative adversarial network trained against the model
explanation: The autoencoder returns here in an interpretability role: force the code to be wide and sparse and each active unit tends to stand for one thing. It is the same machinery as the course's first autoencoder, used to read a model rather than to compress data.

stem: Roughly what share of a Transformer's parameters sits in the feed-forward blocks rather than in attention?
choices: About a tenth
About a quarter
About a half
About two thirds
explanation: Attention gets the attention, but most of the parameters — and on this account most of the stored knowledge — are in the feed-forward layers. That is why they are the main target when a model is being made more efficient.

stem: In a Transformer that has both an encoder and a decoder, what kind of attention joins the two?
choices: Positional attention, which aligns the two sequences by index
Cross-attention in the decoder, which attends to the encoder's representations, while self-attention operates within each side
Self-attention shared between them, with one set of weights
No attention joins them; the encoder's final vector is passed to the decoder
explanation: Self-attention relates a sequence to itself; cross-attention relates the decoder's sequence to the encoder's. Passing one final vector is the older, pre-attention design that the fixed bottleneck problem killed.

stem: Getting a machine to handle language was described in class as 'learn the vocabulary, then learn the grammar'. Which mechanism does each half correspond to?
choices: Vocabulary is the embedding, which gives each word a meaning as a vector; grammar is attention, which works out which words bear on which in this particular sentence
Vocabulary is attention and grammar is the embedding
Vocabulary is tokenisation and grammar is positional encoding
Both halves are handled by the embedding; attention only speeds it up
explanation: Embedding is the dictionary; attention is the syntax. That is the embedding-versus-attention distinction stated as a learning order — global meaning first, local interpretation second.

stem: Attention compares two vectors with a dot product. What does that number tell it?
choices: How many characters the two words share
How far apart the two words sit in the sentence
How congruent the two vectors are — how far they point in the same direction — which becomes how strongly one token should attend to the other
How often the two words occur together in the training corpus
explanation: A dot product is a similarity score: large when two vectors align, near zero when they are unrelated. Attention turns each query-key pair into one of those scores, and those scores are the weights that decide how the value vectors are mixed.

stem: Why is grammar harder for a machine than vocabulary?
choices: Grammar rules change between speakers, while vocabulary does not
A vocabulary is a fixed mapping from word to vector, but grammar needs the context — which word bears on which in this sentence — and that is what attention had to supply
Grammar requires more memory than vocabulary
Vocabulary is learned from data while grammar has to be written by hand
explanation: Word2vec gave every word a stable meaning, but a sentence is more than a bag of meanings: communication comes in sentences and cannot be recovered from distances between isolated words. Attention was the mechanism that added the missing relations.
